chapters.title: Chapter 3: Corporate Tax Rates and Regimes

lessons.title: Reading a Company's Effective Tax Rate on screener.in

body.text: One row on a free website tells you more about a company's tax position than most annual report commentary. Everything in this course so far, the regime choice, the depreciation, the disallowances, the losses and the MAT floor, arrives compressed into a single percentage.

children.text: This lesson is meant to be done with a browser open. Pick any listed company you know, follow the steps, and then read the rest of the lesson against the number you find. The same reading works on your own company's profit and loss account.

body.title: Find the Number, in Six Steps
steps: Open screener.in and search for a company, for example a consumer, IT, cement or auto name you follow
Scroll past the header and quarterly results to the section titled Profit & Loss
Find the row labelled Tax %, sitting directly between Profit before tax and Net Profit
Read the last five years across, not just the latest column
Switch between the standalone and consolidated views using the link near the top, and compare the two
Write down the five-year range and the median, which is the figure worth reasoning about

body.label: screener.in
body.description: Free financials for NSE and BSE listed companies. The Profit & Loss table runs Sales, Expenses, Operating Profit, OPM %, Other Income, Interest, Depreciation, Profit before tax, Tax %, Net Profit, EPS and Dividend Payout %.

body.caption: Tax expense here means current tax plus deferred tax, as charged in the accounts

markDefs.definition: The accounting charge for tax that will arise in future years because of timing differences, such as the gap between book and tax depreciation. It is an accounting entry, not a payment.

children.text: Two things about that formula matter. The numerator is the tax charged in the accounts, which includes
, so it is not the cash the company handed over. And the denominator is book profit, not taxable income, which is precisely why the answer is almost never the headline rate.

stats.label: Most large companies
stats.context: Section 200 [old 115BAA], the benchmark to reason against

stats.label: MAT floor
stats.context: 14% of book profit with 7% surcharge and cess, for old-regime companies

children.text: Reading a Number Below the Benchmark

body.caption: Why a company might show less than 25%

cells: A steady 17% to 18%
The company is a new manufacturer inside section 201 [old 115BAB]
Check when the company was incorporated and when its plant commenced
Low and slowly rising over several years
Brought forward losses being absorbed, common after a turnaround
Look for accumulated losses in the balance sheet and earlier loss years
Low for an IT or export business
A tax holiday unit, historically a special economic zone unit
Segment notes and the tax reconciliation note in the annual report
Consolidated far below standalone
Profits earned in overseas subsidiaries taxed at lower rates
Compare the two views on screener.in directly
One very low year in an otherwise normal series
A deferred tax writeback, or a one-time credit
Read that year's tax note, not the five-year trend
A negative Tax %
A tax credit rather than a charge, usually a deferred tax reversal or a loss year
Confirm profit before tax is positive before drawing any conclusion

body.caption: Why a company might show more than 25%

cells: A steady 33% to 35%
The company never left the old regime, usually because it still has large incentives
26% to 28% in a section 200 company
Permanent disallowances at work: CSR spending, penalties, personal or non-business expenses
A sudden spike in one year
A prior year adjustment, a settled dispute, or a deferred tax charge on a one-time gain
Consolidated above standalone
Loss-making subsidiaries whose losses cannot shelter the parent's profit, or foreign taxes paid abroad
High despite low taxable income
The MAT floor under section 206 [old 115JB] has bitten

body.text: You saw one of these already. The Coimbatore example in Chapter 2 had book profit of ₹1,20,00,000, taxable income of ₹1,24,50,000 after add-backs, and paid ₹31,33,416. Its Tax % would read 26.11% against a headline 25.17%. Nothing exotic happened. CSR spending, a penalty, a cash payment and unpaid supplier dues explained the whole gap.

body.title: Try It: Compute the Rate Yourself
body.prompt: A company reports profit before tax of ₹420 crore and a total tax expense of ₹92 crore. What is its effective tax rate? Answer as a percentage.
body.explanation: 92 divided by 420 is 0.219, so 21.9%. That sits about 3.3 percentage points below the 25.17% benchmark, which on ₹420 crore of profit is roughly ₹13.7 crore of tax not charged. A gap that size is worth explaining rather than admiring: brought forward losses, an overseas subsidiary, or a deferred tax movement would each produce it for very different reasons.

columns.label: Standalone
points: The parent company alone, which is the entity that actually files an Indian return
The cleanest place to see the effect of the Indian regime it has chosen

columns.label: Consolidated
points: The whole group, including foreign and domestic subsidiaries
Blends tax rates from every country the group operates in
A gap between the two views is information, not an error

body.title: Quick Check: What Does the Row Include?
body.question: A company's Tax % row shows 24%. What does that 24% actually measure?
options: The cash tax the company paid to the government during the year
Current tax plus deferred tax, as a share of profit before tax
The statutory rate the company has opted into
Tax on taxable income, as computed in its return
body.explanation: It is the total tax expense in the accounts, current plus deferred, divided by book profit before tax. Cash actually paid appears in the cash flow statement instead, usually as a line like taxes paid. The two differ because deferred tax is an accounting entry and because advance tax and refunds do not follow the accounting year neatly.

children.text: screener.in tells you the what. For the why, every listed company publishes a reconciliation in its annual report, in the notes to accounts, that starts at the statutory rate and walks line by line to its actual effective rate. It is usually a short table, it names the specific items, and almost nobody outside the finance team reads it.

children.text: Search the annual report PDF for the words effective tax rate or reconciliation of tax expense. If you run a private company, ask your auditor to prepare the same table for you once a year. It is the single most useful page of tax analysis a business owner can have.

body.title: Scenario: The Company That Pays 12%
body.scenario: You are looking at a mid-cap engineering company. Its consolidated Tax % reads 11%, 13%, 12%, 26% and 25% across the last five years, most recent first. Standalone reads close to 25% throughout. Profit before tax has grown steadily in every one of those years.
body.prompt: What is most likely going on, and what would you check before concluding anything?
body.modelAnswer: The split between standalone and consolidated is the clue. Standalone sitting near 25% says the Indian parent is an ordinary section 200 [old 115BAA] company with nothing unusual in its own computation. So the low consolidated figure is coming from somewhere inside the group, and the shift from about 25% to about 12% three years ago suggests something specific happened then, rather than a gradual change. The most likely candidates are a subsidiary in a lower-tax jurisdiction that has grown into a meaningful share of group profit, an Indian subsidiary absorbing brought forward losses, or a new manufacturing subsidiary that qualified for section 201 [old 115BAB] at 15%. Three checks settle it. Read the tax reconciliation note in the consolidated accounts, where the difference in subsidiary tax rates appears as its own line. Look at the list of subsidiaries and where they are incorporated. Then check whether anything was acquired or commissioned in the year the rate dropped. What you should not do is treat a low rate as either a red flag or a bonus on its own. A rate built on brought forward losses will rise as those losses run out, while one built on a genuinely low-taxed operating subsidiary may persist, and those two futures look identical in this row.

body.text: Never judge a company on one year of this row. A single year can be distorted by a deferred tax writeback, a settled dispute, a one-time capital gain taxed at a different rate, or an accounting change. Five years and a median tell you about the business. One column tells you about one year.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: What Makes Up the Charge
body.textWithBlank: Total tax expense in the profit and loss account is current tax plus ___ tax, which is why it differs from the cash actually paid during the year.
body.explanation: Deferred tax. It records the tax effect of timing differences, mostly the gap between book and tax depreciation covered in Chapter 2. A company can therefore show a perfectly normal Tax % while paying very little cash tax that year, and the cash flow statement is where you check that.

body.label: Do this for your own company
body.value: Tax expense divided by profit before tax
body.context: Compute it every year and compare it to your regime's headline rate. If the gap is more than two or three percentage points, ask your accountant to name the items. That conversation is where tax planning actually starts.

cards.definition: Total tax expense divided by profit before tax, expressed as a percentage. The Tax % row on screener.in.
Tax on the taxable income of the year, computed under the Income-tax Act.
The accounting charge or credit for timing differences that will reverse in later years. Not a payment.
The parent company alone, which is the entity that files the Indian return.
The parent and all its subsidiaries together, blending tax rates across jurisdictions.
The note in the annual report that walks from the statutory rate to the effective rate, naming each cause.

points: The Tax % row on screener.in sits between Profit before tax and Net Profit, and is total tax expense divided by book profit
It includes deferred tax, so it is not the cash a company paid, which lives in the cash flow statement
Benchmark against 25.17%, or 17.16% for a new manufacturer and about 34.94% for an old-regime company
Rates below the benchmark usually mean brought forward losses, tax holiday units, overseas subsidiaries or a deferred tax movement
Rates above it usually mean permanent disallowances, old-regime rates, prior year adjustments or the MAT floor
Read standalone and consolidated side by side, and read five years rather than one
The annual report's tax reconciliation note names the exact causes, and you can ask your own auditor for the same table

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and is not investment or tax advice. A company's effective tax rate is one data point among many and should never drive an investment decision on its own. Third party websites present data in their own way and can contain errors, so verify anything important against the company's own audited financial statements.
